extraction.name: MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms
extraction.description: We introduce a large-scale dataset of math word problems and an interpretable neural math problem solver that learns to map problems to operation programs.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
extraction.publisher: University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI
extraction.citeAs: Amini, A., Gabriel, S., Lin, S., Koncel-Kedziorski, R., Choi, Y., & Hajishirzi, H. (2019). MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv:1905.13319.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: We use problems in the AQuA dataset and carefully annotate those problems with formal operation programs. We use crowdsourcing to carefully align problems with operation programs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Math problems are first categorized into math domains using term frequencies. These domains are used to prune the search space of possible operations to align with the word problem text.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators are provided with a problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments. They iteratively select operations and arguments until the problem is solved. The platform only accepts programs which include some numbers from the problem, and whose final calculation is very close to the correct numeric solution.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: We leverage a validation strategy to check whether the problems and annotated programs are aligned or not. According to this strategy, at least 2 out of 3 validators should rank the operation program as valid for it to be selected. The validation accuracy is 94.64% across categories.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Our representation language does not cover high-order polynomials and problems where the solutions are entirely nonnumeric. Some errors are due to limitations in our representation language (e.g., factorization operation not defined).
